extracted.intended_audience: citizens, legislators, and interpreters assessing the proposed U.S. Constitution's allocation of taxation and sovereign powers
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles and interpretive rules for deciding whether particular fiscal and legislative powers are exclusive to the national government or concurrent with the States, and for assessing the prudential design of revenue powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on structure not power extent for usurpation fears
rubrics_metrics.description: “All observations founded upon the danger of usurpation ought to be referred to the composition and structure of the government, not to the nature or extent of its powers.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating risks of usurpation, examine how governments are constituted and the dependence of officeholders on the people (manner of formation, popular control), rather than merely cataloging the formal extent of grants of power. If the federal structure affords the same species of security as the States' constitutions, fears of usurpation should be discarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive delegation — three cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusive delegation of State sovereignty to the Union exists only in three cases: (1) where the Constitution expressly grants exclusive authority to the Union; (2) where it grants an authority to the Union in one clause and elsewhere prohibits the States from exercising the like authority; and (3) where the grant to the Union would be absolutely and totally contradictory and repugnant to a similar State authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these three tests as a rule of interpretation to determine whether a power is solely federal. Examples supplied: (1) 'exclusive legislation' over the federal district (express grant); (2) duties on imports (grant to Congress plus prohibition on States) illustrating the second case; (3) 'to establish a uniform rule of naturalization' illustrating the third case (uniformity would be impossible if States prescribed distinct rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent jurisdiction for internal taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of imposing taxes on all articles other than exports and imports is a concurrent and coequal authority in the United States and in the individual States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent an express granting clause making the power exclusive, or an independent prohibitory clause, internal taxation should be read as concurrent. Use textual indicators (e.g., prohibitions that imply retained powers) and the overall structure of the Constitution to support concurrency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative-pregnant interpretation (prohibition implies affirmation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A restraining or prohibitory clause (e.g., forbidding States from laying duties on imports/exports) may amount to what lawyers call a 'negative pregnant' — a negation of one thing and an affirmation of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret prohibitions carefully: an explicit prohibition of a particular State power often implies that other powers (not mentioned) remain with the States. It is sophistry to read a prohibition as evidence that all other similar powers were intended to be subtracted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repugnancy standard for implied exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere possibility of inconvenience or that a State tax might make a federal tax inexpedient does not imply constitutional inability; only an immediate constitutional repugnancy can, by implication, alienate and extinguish a pre-existing right of sovereignty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish prudential conflicts (expediency or policy clashes) from constitutional contradictions. Only direct, irreconcilable contradiction between a federal grant and a State exercise will imply exclusion; occasional policy interference does not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary and Proper clause is declaratory
rubrics_metrics.description: The clause authorizing Congress 'to make all laws which shall be NECESSARY and PROPER for carrying into execution the powers vested' is 'only declaratory of a truth' — a power to do an act implies the power to employ the means necessary to execute it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the Necessary and Proper clause as an affirming statement that the means incidental to an expressly granted power belong to the government possessing that power. Assess whether a law is a proper means to execute an expressly granted federal power rather than treating the clause as creating new, independent powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial judgement of necessity by government; final by the people
rubrics_metrics.description: The national government must judge, in the first instance, of the proper exercise of its powers; its constituents (the people) must judge in the last instance and redress usurpations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In disputes over whether a federal act is 'necessary and proper' or exceeds authority, give initial deference to the national government's judgment but recognize popular sovereignty as the ultimate corrective. Political remedies and the people's prudent measures are the final check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supremacy limited to laws 'in pursuance' of the Constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: The clause making the Constitution and laws 'the SUPREME LAW of the land' expressly confines that supremacy to laws made 'IN PURSUANCE' of the Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not read the supremacy clause as validating federal acts not enacted pursuant to constitutional powers; such acts are usurpations and do not become valid by virtue of being labeled federal law. Always test federal laws against the scope of constitutional grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: State revenue authority retained except imports/exports
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual States retain an independent and uncontrollable authority to raise revenue for their own wants by every kind of taxation, with the sole exception of duties on imports and exports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing state fiscal powers under the proposed Constitution, assume broad residual taxing authority unless the text explicitly removes it (as with duties on imports/exports). This supports a substantial independent revenue capacity for States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent jurisdiction preferred to complete subordination
rubrics_metrics.description: A concurrent jurisdiction in the article of taxation was the only admissible substitute for an entire subordination, in respect to this branch of power, of State authority to that of the Union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer arrangements that allow both levels to tax (concurrent jurisdiction) rather than complete state subordination to national fiscal control; concurrency reconciles an indefinite federal taxing power with adequate state resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid restricting federal taxation to particular objects
rubrics_metrics.description: If the jurisdiction of the national government in revenue were restricted to particular objects (e.g., duties on imports), it would occasion two evils: the oppression of particular branches of industry and an unequal distribution of taxes among states and citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design revenue powers with a sufficiently broad base to prevent overburdening particular industries or regions. Beware schemes that force the government to rely on narrow sources (like imports) which incentivize excessive rates and produce unfair burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks of excessive import duties (smuggling, monopolies, merchant oppression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exorbitant duties on imported articles would beget a general spirit of smuggling; tend to render other classes tributary to manufacturing classes (premature monopolies); sometimes force industry into less advantageous channels; and often oppress the merchant who may bear duties without retribution from the consumer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When considering reliance on import duties, factor in secondary harms: enforcement difficulties (smuggling), distortion of industry and markets (premature monopolies), and unfair incidence on intermediaries (merchants). These practical outcomes argue against concentrating revenue on imports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design constitutions for future contingencies, not just present exigencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutions of civil government are not to be framed upon a calculation of existing exigencies, but upon a combination of these with the probable exigencies of ages; there ought to be a capacity to provide for future contingencies (e.g., defense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When allocating governmental taxing powers, account for unforeseeable future needs (national defense, large-scale crises). Avoid rigid textual limits that would incapacitate the government from responding to future exigencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish prudential questions from constitutional limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The quantity of the imposition, the expediency or inexpediency of an increase on either side, would be mutually questions of prudence; but there would be involved no direct contradiction of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate policy/prudence judgments (how much tax is wise) from constitutional questions (whether a power exists). Do not convert disagreements about expediency into claims that a power is constitutionally impossible.
